attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, written in his own voice. Nobody else is being quoted.

semantics.note: The sentence follows straight on from 'The likely outcome here?' and continues the list of consequences, so it is hedged as a likely outcome. The drafter's firm 'will' drops that hedge. The causal link to GenAI cheating is kept correctly.

contract.note: The contract scores this on a plain reading as if it were a firm forecast. That ignores the 'likely outcome' framing that governs the passage. Plain-reading scoring applies only to firm language, so the contract is not fair to the speaker's actual words.

evidence.note: A 2024 survey of students at UC campuses where about 9% of AI users admitted cheating with it. This bears only on the condition (that cheating happens), not on whether employers struggle to hire, so it cannot support the claim.

A 2026 NACE survey of 185 employers says new graduates are largely prepared, with weaknesses in critical thinking. It measures a different thing (preparedness ratings, not hiring difficulty) and does not test the cheating link, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Marcus presents this as part of 'the likely outcome', a probabilistic hedge, so under policy it is not scored. Even read as a firm forecast, it has no deadline, and the packet has no evidence that employers broadly struggle to hire because of learning lost to GenAI cheating. That would leave it unresolved, not contradicted.
